data.name: We Slay Monsters
data.detailed_description:
We Slay Monsters streamlines traditional roguelike RPG gameplay and introduces a unique poker-esque card based combat mechanic. Each class (Wizard, Rogue, Warrior) has a unique deck of cards; using this deck you will guide your hero through the dungeon. Each dungeon is designed to play in short bursts, with a single dungeon taking 15-25 minutes to complete (or even less if your hero dies).

The Academy For Dungeoneering

In We Slay Monsters, the player is tasked with the rebuilding of the once prestigious Academy For Dungeoneering, famous for training generations of heroes, but long since fallen into disrepair.

The Academy is your persistent base that can be upgraded over time with gold earned by performing successful quests for nearby towns. Heroes may die, but your Academy lives on.

Features
  • Poker-esque card-based combat mechanic. Most hands that would be valid in poker are valid here, except the deck is made up of six suits instead of four, with face values from 1-9 instead of Ace-King. Flushes can be made with only three of the same suit, and any flush results in a super attack. Each suit has a unique attack ability.
  • Campaign against the Institute of Evil. In the campaign, you square off against the Institute of Evil, a rival school responsible for training evil beasts and strange bosses to take over the world.
  • Endless supply of recruits. Permadeath means a hero might die, but your Academy has an endless supply of new recruits willing to risk all for fame and fortune.
  • Over 35 monsters which can be unlocked. Each monster has unique abilities, and monsters are unlocked over time as you complete quests.

Soundtrack

Our composer Adam Chandler has done a great job with the music and sound effects for the game, and the full soundtrack album is available as DLC for the game, or buy the game with the soundtrack and save 10%!

reviews.review:
We Slay Monsters takes an unusual approach to the roguelike dungeon crawler by combining fantasy adventuring with a combat system inspired by poker. Instead of relying on conventional turn-based commands or action-heavy battles, it asks players to build useful card combinations and turn those hands into attacks. Developed and published by Furiously Inactive Games, the game has a relatively compact scope, but its distinctive mechanics give it an identity that separates it from more traditional dungeon-crawling RPGs.

Players can adventure as a Wizard, Rogue, or Warrior, with each class receiving its own deck and combat characteristics. Cards are numbered from 1 through 9 and divided among six suits, with different combinations determining the effectiveness of attacks. Familiar concepts such as flushes appear, although the rules are adjusted specifically for the game's combat system rather than following real poker exactly. This makes the mechanics approachable even for players who have little interest in poker while still rewarding those who enjoy probability, hand management, and tactical decision-making.

Combat becomes particularly engaging when a less-than-perfect selection of cards forces improvisation. Strong combinations can produce powerful results, but players cannot depend entirely on drawing ideal hands. Choosing how to work with available cards becomes part of the challenge. The class-specific decks also prevent the three heroes from feeling interchangeable, encouraging players to learn their individual strengths and discover which approach best suits their preferred style.

A major part of the larger progression system revolves around the Academy for Dungeoneering. Once a prestigious institution for training adventurers, the Academy has declined and needs to be restored. Gold earned by completing quests can be invested into its development, creating persistent advancement between dungeon expeditions. This gives players something meaningful to pursue even when individual adventurers eventually meet unfortunate ends.

Permadeath plays an important role in establishing the game's roguelike character. Heroes can be permanently lost, making dangerous encounters carry genuine consequences. Fortunately, recruits remain available, so losing one character does not bring the entire campaign to a halt. The combination of disposable adventurers and a persistent Academy creates a sensible balance between punishment and progression. A failed run can sting without making all previous effort feel pointless.

Individual dungeon runs are intentionally brief, typically designed around sessions lasting roughly 15 to 25 minutes. This makes We Slay Monsters easy to enjoy in smaller bursts and encourages repeated attempts. The shorter format works particularly well with the randomized nature of its combat because trying another class or experimenting with different card decisions does not demand a huge time commitment. On the other hand, players looking for enormous procedural worlds or exceptionally elaborate RPG development may find its structure comparatively limited.

The campaign adds some personality through the conflict surrounding the Institute of Evil, an organization responsible for training monsters and bosses. As progress continues, more than 35 monsters can become available, expanding the variety of enemies encountered during quests. Different creatures bring individual abilities into battle, gradually requiring players to adapt their strategies instead of relying indefinitely on the same successful card combinations.

Its presentation favors charm and accessibility over spectacle. The fantasy theme has a playful quality that suits the unusual premise, while Adam Chandler's music and sound effects help give dungeon expeditions additional character. Steam achievements, leaderboards, Steam Cloud functionality, and trading cards add secondary incentives for players interested in completing challenges or comparing their performance.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially categorized as Playable rather than fully Verified. Performance with the default graphics configuration is considered suitable, and the game can run successfully on SteamOS. However, handheld players should expect compromises. Some functionality is not fully accessible through the default controller configuration, touchscreen interaction or a community controller layout may occasionally be useful, and text entry can require manually opening the virtual keyboard. Some interface text may also appear small, while certain prompts can display keyboard, mouse, or non-Steam Deck controller icons. It is therefore functional on the Deck, but the experience is less seamless than a fully optimized handheld release.

We Slay Monsters ultimately works best for players who appreciate compact roguelikes built around one distinctive mechanical idea. Its modified poker combat is the centerpiece and successfully transforms familiar card combinations into a tactical battle system. The persistent Academy makes character losses easier to accept, while three classes, randomized adventures, unlockable monsters, and short dungeon sessions provide reasons to return. Its limited scale and relatively straightforward progression keep it from offering the enormous depth found in more ambitious roguelikes, but the focused design also prevents unnecessary complexity.

As a small-scale combination of card strategy, fantasy dungeon crawling, persistent progression, and permadeath, it remains an interesting experiment with enough personality to justify multiple runs. Players attracted to unconventional combat systems are likely to get the most from it, particularly if they prefer shorter roguelike sessions rather than lengthy campaigns built around individual characters.

Rating: 7/10
